es: Para algo que empezó y sigue, usa *since* con el presente perfecto: *I have lived here since 2019.*
en: For something that started and continues, use *since* with the present perfect: *I have lived here since 2019.*

es: *People* ya es plural, no digas *peoples*: *People are nice*, nunca *People is nice*.
en: *People* is already plural; say *People are nice*, never *People is nice* or *peoples*.

es: No digas *explain me*; el verbo necesita *to*: *Can you explain this to me?*
en: Don't say *explain me*; the verb needs *to*: *Can you explain this to me?*

es: *Depend* siempre va con *on*: *It depends on the weather*, nunca *depend of*.
en: *Depend* always takes *on*: say *It depends on the weather*, never *depend of*.

es: Con *he*, *she* o *it* en presente, el verbo lleva *-s*: *She works on Mondays.*
en: With *he*, *she* or *it* in the present, add *-s*: *She works on Mondays.*

es: Para preguntas en presente usa *do* o *does*: *Does she speak English?*, no *Speaks she English?*
en: Use *do* or *does* for present-tense questions: *Does she speak English?*, not *Speaks she English?*

es: *A* o *an* dependen del sonido, no de la letra: *an hour*, pero *a university*.
en: *A* or *an* depends on the sound, not the letter: *an hour*, but *a university*.

es: En inglés el adjetivo va antes del sustantivo: *a red car*, no *a car red*.
en: In English, the adjective goes before the noun: *a red car*, not *a car red*.

es: Para hablar en general, no uses artículo con plurales: *Dogs are loyal*, no *The dogs are loyal.*
en: When speaking generally, skip the article with plurals: *Dogs are loyal*, not *The dogs are loyal.*

es: *Advice* e *information* son incontables: di *some advice*, nunca *an advice* o *advices*.
en: *Advice* and *information* are uncountable: say *some advice*, never *an advice* or *advices*.

es: *News* se ve plural pero es incontable: *The news is good*, no *The news are good.*
en: *News* looks plural but is uncountable: *The news is good*, not *The news are good.*

es: Usa *simple past* con una fecha exacta y *present perfect* cuando el momento no importa.
en: Use the *simple past* for a specific time and the *present perfect* when the exact time doesn't matter.

es: Para hábitos pasados que ya no existen, usa *used to*: *I used to play football.*
en: For past habits that no longer happen, use *used to*: *I used to play football.*

es: Adjetivos cortos usan *-er*: *bigger*; los largos usan *more*: *more interesting.*
en: Short adjectives take *-er*: *bigger*; longer ones take *more*: *more interesting.*

es: *Much* va con incontables y *many* con contables: *much time*, *many friends.*
en: *Much* goes with uncountables and *many* with countables: *much time*, *many friends.*

es: Usa *some* en afirmaciones y *any* en negativas y preguntas: *I have some money* / *Do you have any money?*
en: Use *some* in statements and *any* in negatives and questions: *I have some money* / *Do you have any money?*

es: Usa *going to* para planes ya decididos y *will* para decisiones del momento.
en: Use *going to* for plans already decided and *will* for decisions made on the spot.

es: El primer condicional usa *if* + presente y *will*: *If it rains, I will stay home.*
en: The first conditional uses *if* + present and *will*: *If it rains, I will stay home.*

es: Para situaciones hipotéticas usa *if* + pasado y *would*: *If I won the lottery, I would travel.*
en: For hypothetical situations, use *if* + past and *would*: *If I won the lottery, I would travel.*

es: La voz pasiva usa *be* + participio: *The book was written in 1990*, cuando el agente no importa.
en: The passive voice uses *be* + past participle: *The book was written in 1990*, when the agent doesn't matter.

es: *Make* es crear algo y *do* es realizar una actividad: *make a cake*, *do homework.*
en: *Make* means creating something and *do* means performing an activity: *make a cake*, *do homework.*

es: *Tell* necesita a quién: *tell me*; *say* no: *say something.*
en: *Tell* needs an object: *tell me*; *say* doesn't: *say something.*

es: *Borrow* es pedir prestado y *lend* es prestar: *Can I borrow your pen?* / *I'll lend you mine.*
en: *Borrow* means to take and *lend* means to give: *Can I borrow your pen?* / *I'll lend you mine.*

es: *Bring* es traer algo hacia aquí y *take* es llevarlo hacia allá.
en: *Bring* means moving something here, and *take* means moving it there.

es: *Look like* describe apariencia: *You look like your dad*; *look at* es mirar algo.
en: *Look like* describes appearance: *You look like your dad*; *look at* means to view something.

es: *Hear* es oír sin querer y *listen* es escuchar con atención: *listen to music.*
en: *Hear* means noticing a sound and *listen* means paying attention: *listen to music.*

es: *See* es ver algo y *watch* es observar algo que se mueve: *watch a movie.*
en: *See* means noticing something, and *watch* means observing something moving: *watch a movie.*

es: *Travel* es el verbo, *a trip* es el viaje de ida y vuelta, y *a journey* enfatiza el recorrido: *a long journey.*
en: *Travel* is the verb, *a trip* is going somewhere and coming back, and *a journey* stresses the route: *a long journey.*

es: *Job* es un empleo específico y *work* es la actividad en general: *I have a new job.*
en: *A job* is a specific position and *work* is the activity in general: *I have a new job.*

es: *House* es el edificio y *home* es el hogar, con sentido emocional: *Home sweet home.*
en: *House* is the building and *home* is where you belong emotionally: *Home sweet home.*

es: *Clothes* es la ropa, siempre plural, y *cloth* es la tela, la materia prima.
en: *Clothes* means garments, always plural, and *cloth* means fabric, the raw material.

es: *Weather* es el clima y *time* es el tiempo que pasa: no confundas ambos con *tiempo*.
en: *Weather* means climate and *time* means duration: Spanish *tiempo* covers both words.

es: *Remember* es recordar tú mismo y *remind* es hacer que otro recuerde: *Remind me to call her.*
en: *Remember* means recalling yourself and *remind* means making someone else recall: *Remind me to call her.*

es: *Meet* es conocer por primera vez y *know* es ya conocer a alguien.
en: *Meet* means encountering someone for the first time, and *know* means already being acquainted.

es: *Actually* no significa *actualmente*; significa *en realidad*: *Actually, I disagree.*
en: *Actually* doesn't mean 'currently'; it means 'in fact': *Actually, I disagree.*

es: *Embarrassed* significa *avergonzado*, no *embarazada*. Para eso usa *pregnant.*
en: *Embarrassed* means ashamed, not pregnant. For that meaning, use *pregnant.*

es: *Library* es la *biblioteca*; la librería donde compras libros es *bookstore.*
en: *Library* means a place to borrow books; a shop that sells them is a *bookstore.*

es: *Assist* significa *ayudar*, no *asistir* a un evento; para eso usa *attend.*
en: *Assist* means to help, not to attend an event; for that, use *attend.*

es: *Attend* significa *asistir* a algo, como una clase o reunión: *attend a meeting.*
en: *Attend* means to be present at something, like a class or meeting: *attend a meeting.*

es: *Realize* significa *darse cuenta*, no *realizar* una tarea; para eso usa *carry out* o *do.*
en: *Realize* means to become aware, not to carry out a task; for that, use *do* or *carry out.*

es: *Constipated* significa *estreñido*; si tienes un resfriado, di *I have a cold.*
en: *Constipated* refers to digestion; if you have a cold, say *I have a cold*, not *I'm constipated.*

es: *Exit* es la *salida* de un lugar; el *éxito* en inglés se dice *success.*
en: *Exit* means the way out; achievement in Spanish is *éxito*, which is *success* in English.

es: *Success* es *éxito*; no lo confundas con *suceso*, que se traduce como *event.*
en: *Success* means achievement; don't confuse it with *suceso*, an event, which is *event* in English.

es: *Carpet* es la *alfombra*; la carpeta de documentos se dice *folder* o *file.*
en: *Carpet* means a rug; a document folder is a *folder*, not a *carpet.*

es: *Fabric* significa *tela*; una fábrica donde se produce algo es *factory.*
en: *Fabric* means cloth; a place that manufactures goods is a *factory.*

es: *Lecture* es una clase magistral o charla, no una lectura; para leer usa *reading.*
en: *Lecture* means a formal talk, not reading; the act of reading is simply *reading.*

es: *Pretend* significa *fingir*, no *pretender*; para eso usa *intend* o *try to.*
en: *Pretend* means to fake something, not to intend; for that, use *intend* or *try to.*

es: *Sensible* significa sensato; para la persona sensible o delicada usa *sensitive*: *She is very sensitive.*
en: *Sensible* means practical and wise; for the emotional sense, use *sensitive* instead.

es: *Eventually* significa *finalmente*, no *eventualmente*; para eso usa *occasionally.*
en: *Eventually* means 'in the end', not 'occasionally'; for that sense, use *occasionally.*

es: *Career* es la *carrera profesional*; una carrera universitaria se dice *degree* o *major.*
en: *Career* means your professional path; a university degree program is called a *degree* or *major.*

es: La edad se dice con *to be*, no *have*: *I am 20 years old*, nunca *I have 20 years.*
en: Say your age with *to be*, not *have*: *I am 20 years old*, never *I have 20 years.*

es: Para las comidas usa *have*, no *take*: *I have breakfast at 7*, no *I take breakfast.*
en: Use *have* for meals, not *take*: *I have breakfast at 7*, not *I take breakfast.*

es: *Agree* es un verbo por sí mismo: di *I agree*, nunca *I am agree.*
en: *Agree* is a verb on its own: say *I agree*, never *I am agree.*

es: Las preguntas se hacen con *ask*, no con *make*: *ask a question*, nunca *make a question.*
en: Use *ask* with questions, not *make*: *ask a question*, never *make a question.*

es: *Bored* describe cómo te sientes y *boring* describe la cosa aburrida: *I'm bored because the movie is boring.*
en: *Bored* describes how you feel and *boring* describes the dull thing: *I'm bored because the movie is boring.*

es: En inglés evita la doble negación: di *I don't have any money*, no *I don't have no money.*
en: English avoids double negatives: say *I don't have any money*, not *I don't have no money.*

es: Para responder, usa *I think so* o *I don't think so*, no *I think yes.*
en: To answer briefly, use *I think so* or *I don't think so*, not *I think yes.*

es: No pongas artículo con posesivo: di *my book*, nunca *my the book.*
en: Don't add an article with a possessive: say *my book*, never *my the book.*

es: No abuses de *very*; usa palabras más fuertes: *huge* en vez de *very big*, *exhausted* en vez de *very tired.*
en: Don’t overuse *very*; pick stronger words: *huge* instead of *very big*, *exhausted* instead of *very tired.*

es: Los adverbios de frecuencia van antes del verbo principal: *I always drink coffee*, no *I drink always coffee.*
en: Frequency adverbs go before the main verb: *I always drink coffee*, not *I drink always coffee.*

es: Después de *want* usa *to*: *I want to go*, nunca *I want go.*
en: After the verb *want*, use *to*: *I want to go*, never *I want go.*

es: Después de *can* el verbo va sin *to*: *I can swim*, nunca *I can to swim.*
en: After *can*, the verb has no *to*: *I can swim*, never *I can to swim.*

es: *Good* es adjetivo y *well* es adverbio: *She sings well*, no *She sings good.*
en: *Good* is an adjective and *well* is an adverb: *She sings well*, not *She sings good.*

es: Después de *enjoy* siempre usa *-ing*: *I enjoy swimming*, nunca *I enjoy to swim.*
en: After *enjoy*, always use *-ing*: *I enjoy swimming*, never *I enjoy to swim.*

es: *Excited* describe cómo te sientes y *exciting* describe lo emocionante: *The trip is exciting, so I'm excited.*
en: *Excited* describes your feeling and *exciting* describes the thing: *The trip is exciting, so I'm excited.*

es: Sensaciones como hambre o frío se dicen con *to be*: *I'm hungry*, *I'm cold*, nunca *I have hunger.*
en: Feelings like hunger or cold use *to be*: *I'm hungry*, *I'm cold*, never *I have hunger.*

es: El final *-ed* suena /t/, /d/ o /ɪd/: *worked* con /t/, *played* con /d/, *wanted* con /ɪd/.
en: The *-ed* ending sounds like /t/, /d/, or /ɪd/: *worked* with /t/, *played* with /d/, *wanted* with /ɪd/.

es: El sonido *th* no existe en español: pon la lengua entre los dientes para *think*, distinto de *sink.*
en: The *th* sound has no Spanish equivalent: put your tongue between your teeth for *think*, unlike *sink.*

es: Muchas palabras tienen letras mudas: la *k* de *knife* y la *h* de *honest* no se pronuncian.
en: Many words have silent letters: the *k* in *knife* and the *h* in *honest* aren't pronounced.

es: Algunas palabras cambian el acento según sean sustantivo o verbo: *RECord* como sustantivo y *reCORD* como verbo.
en: Some words shift stress between noun and verb: *RECord* as a noun versus *reCORD* as a verb.

es: La *v* y la *b* suenan distinto en inglés: en *very*, los dientes de arriba tocan el labio de abajo.
en: *V* and *b* sound different in English: in *very*, your top teeth touch your bottom lip.

es: La *h* inglesa casi siempre suena, como una *j* suave: *hotel*, *house*. Excepciones: *hour*, *honest.*
en: The English *h* is usually pronounced, like a soft breath: *hotel*, *house*. Exceptions: *hour*, *honest.*

es: La *s* final suena distinto según la palabra: *cats* con /s/, *dogs* con /z/, *watches* con /ɪz/.
en: The final *s* has different sounds: *cats* with /s/, *dogs* with /z/, *watches* with /ɪz/.

es: *Ship* y *sheep* suenan distinto: una *i* corta frente a un sonido *ee* largo.
en: *Ship* and *sheep* sound different: a short *i* sound versus a long *ee* sound.

es: La *w* en inglés no suena como *gu* en español: redondea los labios para *woman*, no digas *guoman.*
en: English *w* isn't a Spanish *gu* sound: round your lips for *woman*, not *guoman.*

es: La *r* en inglés no se vibra como en español: en *red*, la lengua no toca el paladar.
en: English *r* isn't rolled like Spanish: in *red*, your tongue doesn't touch the roof of your mouth.

es: *Look for* significa *buscar algo*: *I'm looking for my keys everywhere.*
en: *Look for* means to search for something: *I'm looking for my keys everywhere.*

es: *Turn off* significa *apagar*: *Turn off the lights before you leave.*
en: *Turn off* means to switch something off: *Turn off the lights before you leave.*

es: *Give up* significa *rendirse* o *dejar algo*: *Don't give up on your dreams.*
en: *Give up* means to quit or stop trying: *Don't give up on your dreams.*

es: *Find out* significa *descubrir* información: *I found out the truth yesterday.*
en: *Find out* means to discover information: *I found out the truth yesterday.*

es: *Run out of* significa *quedarse sin algo*: *We ran out of milk.*
en: *Run out of* means to have no more of something: *We ran out of milk.*

es: *Get up* significa *levantarse* de la cama: *I get up at 7 every day.*
en: *Get up* means to rise from bed: *I get up at 7 o'clock every day.*

es: *Put off* significa *posponer*: *Don't put off your homework until tomorrow.*
en: *Put off* means to postpone: *Don't put off your homework until tomorrow.*

es: *Come across* significa *encontrarse con algo* por casualidad: *I came across an old photo.*
en: *Come across* means to find something by chance: *I came across an old photo.*

es: *Look after* significa *cuidar de alguien*: *Can you look after my dog?*
en: *Look after* means to take care of someone: *Can you look after my dog?*

es: *Break down* significa *dejar de funcionar*: *My car broke down on the highway.*
en: *Break down* means to stop working: *My car broke down on the highway.*

es: *Could you...?* suena más cortés que *Can you...?* para pedir favores: *Could you help me, please?*
en: *Could you...?* sounds more polite than *Can you...?* for asking favors: *Could you help me, please?*

es: *How come?* significa *¿cómo es que...?* y va seguido del orden normal: *How come you're here?*
en: *How come?* means 'why' in a casual way, followed by normal word order: *How come you're here?*

es: *I'm afraid not* es una forma educada de decir *no*: *Can you come? I'm afraid not.*
en: *I'm afraid not* is a polite way to say no: *Can you come? I'm afraid not.*

es: *It's up to you* significa *la decisión es tuya*: *We can go now or later, it's up to you.*
en: *It's up to you* means the choice is yours: *We can go now or later, it's up to you.*

es: *Long time no see* se usa para saludar a alguien que no ves hace tiempo.
en: *Long time no see* is a casual greeting for someone you haven't seen in a while.

es: *Take your time* significa *tómate tu tiempo*: nadie te está apurando, así que relájate.
en: *Take your time* means there's no rush at all, so relax and go at your own pace.

es: *No worries* es una forma informal de decir *no te preocupes* o *de nada.*
en: *No worries* is a casual way to say *don't worry* or *you're welcome.*

es: *Let me know* significa *avísame*: *Let me know if you need anything.*
en: *Let me know* means 'tell me later': *Let me know if you need anything.*

es: *Its* es posesivo y *it's* es *it is*: *The dog wagged its tail* vs *It's raining.*
en: *Its* is possessive and *it's* means *it is*: *The dog wagged its tail* vs *It's raining.*

es: *Then* indica tiempo y *than* se usa en comparaciones: *First this, then that* vs *better than this.*
en: *Then* refers to time and *than* is for comparisons: *First this, then that* vs *better than this.*

es: En inglés, *I*, los días y los meses siempre van con mayúscula: *Monday*, *January.*
en: In English, *I*, days, and months are always capitalized: *Monday*, *January.*

es: Si un verbo corto termina en consonante-vocal-consonante, dobla la última: *stop* → *stopped*, *run* → *running.*
en: If a short verb ends consonant-vowel-consonant, double the last letter: *stop* → *stopped*, *run* → *running.*

es: Si el verbo termina en *e* muda, quítala antes de *-ing*: *write* se vuelve *writing.*
en: If a verb ends in a silent *e*, drop it before *-ing*: *write* becomes *writing.*

es: *There*, *their* y *they're* suenan igual pero significan distinto: lugar, posesión y *they are.*
en: *There*, *their*, and *they're* sound the same but differ: place, possession, and *they are.*
